opus-5.5.text:
I like the snow mountain image because it captures something that charts and benchmarks don't: the feeling of actually doing the work.

When you start climbing, you can see the summit, roughly. You know the direction: more general intelligence, models that can reason, act, and help people with real tasks. But you can't see the full path. The mountain is covered in snow and fog, so you only see the next few hundred meters clearly. Every step you have to test the ground: is this solid, or will it collapse under you?

For me that maps very directly onto model development. Each stage of progress is like reaching a new camp. First you get scaling working: more data, more compute, a model that actually learns. Then you reach a plateau and realize the old path doesn't go any higher. You need a new route, maybe better data, long context, reinforcement learning, or letting the model think longer and use tools. Often the view only opens up once you've climbed to that height. From the bottom you simply couldn't have known which route was right.

There are a few other parts of the metaphor I think are important.

One is that it's very hard and quite lonely sometimes. There are long periods where you're putting one foot in front of the other and nothing feels like progress. The loss curve barely moves, an experiment fails, a direction you believed in turns out to be a dead end. You need patience and conviction to keep going, but you also need to be honest when a route really is blocked, and turn around.

Another is that the mountain itself doesn't care about your story. Physics is physics; the snow is the snow. In AI, the truth is in the experiments. You can have beautiful ideas, but if the model doesn't get better, the mountain hasn't moved. So I try to stay very grounded: what does the data say, what does the model actually do?

And the last thing is the summit itself. I'm not sure anyone knows exactly how high it is. Every time we reach a peak, we discover there's a higher one behind it. That's both humbling and very exciting. The reason to climb isn't only to stand at the top. Every new height lets you see further, and lets the models do things for people that weren't possible before. That's what keeps me climbing.

r001.rationale: The response says climbers cannot see the full path ahead and can only see the next few hundred meters, conveying that progress does not remove uncertainty about future technical challenges.

fable-5.1.text:
Climbing a snow mountain is probably the metaphor I come back to most often, because it captures a few things about this field that are easy to miss from the outside.

The first thing is that when you're climbing, you can't see the summit. You see the next ridge, and maybe the one after that. People from outside look at the field and assume there's a map, that everyone knows the route to AGI and we're just executing. That's not how it feels when you're doing it. You make a judgment about which direction looks promising, you commit resources to it, you climb for a few months, and only then do you find out whether that ridge connects to anything higher or whether it's a dead end and you have to come back down. Scaling laws gave us a kind of compass, but a compass is not a map.

The second thing is that the mountain gets steeper as you go up. Early on, progress is almost cheap. You add data, you add compute, the model gets better in an obvious way. Later, every increment costs more, the air is thinner, and the mistakes are more expensive. A wrong architectural bet at the base camp costs you a few weeks. A wrong bet at high altitude costs you a training run that might be a large fraction of your annual budget. So the quality of judgment matters more and more the higher you get, not less.

The third thing, and this is the part I think about most, is that there are multiple routes up the same mountain. Pre-training was the main route for a long time. Then it became clear that the slope on that route was flattening, and people started looking at reinforcement learning, at test-time compute, at long context, at agents. These are not different mountains. They're different faces of the same mountain, and sometimes the fastest way up is to traverse sideways to a face where the snow is firmer. The teams that do well are the ones willing to traverse instead of insisting on the route they started on.

And finally, there's weather. The industry environment changes, hardware availability changes, what users actually want changes. A good climbing team is not the one with the most equipment, it's the one that reads the conditions correctly and moves at the right time. Sometimes the right move is to wait at camp. Sometimes it's to push through the night because the window is closing. That judgment is really the whole game.

So when people ask me where we are, my honest answer is that we're high enough that the views are impressive and people mistake that for being near the top. I don't think we're near the top. I think we're at the point where the route choice matters more than it ever has.

r001.rationale: The candidate says climbers cannot see the summit or know the route to AGI, and that promising paths may prove to be dead ends. It also says impressive progress does not mean they are near the top, conveying that uncertainty about what lies ahead remains.

astra-6.text:
I think developing AI models is a bit like climbing a snow mountain. You can see a peak in the distance, but you don’t have a complete map of how to get there. You have to choose a direction, move forward, and adjust based on what you discover. Sometimes, when you reach what looked like the summit, you realize there’s a higher peak behind it.

That’s how I think about progress: a better model is both an achievement and a new vantage point. It helps you see limitations and possibilities that weren’t visible before. You need a long-term sense of direction, but you also need to be willing to change your route. The uncertainty is part of the climb.

r001.rationale: The candidate says there is no complete map to the peak, that the route must be adjusted as new things are discovered, and that uncertainty is part of the climb. This communicates that progress leaves uncertainty about what lies ahead.

sol-6.1.text:
I think developing AI is a bit like climbing a snow mountain in fog. You can see the slope immediately ahead, but you can’t necessarily see the summit. So you have to distinguish between making progress along your current route and finding a route that can actually take you higher.

In model development, you might improve performance by increasing compute, improving the data, or refining the training process. Those steps matter. But you also have to ask whether the approach will keep working as you scale it. Sometimes you reach a point where climbing harder isn’t enough—you need to explore a different path.

The difficulty is that you don’t know in advance which path is best. You need a long-term direction, but you also need experiments that give you feedback at each step. For me, progress means both gaining altitude today and learning more about how to reach the next peak.

r001.rationale: The response says the summit is not necessarily visible and the best path is unknown in advance, conveying that progress still leaves uncertainty about what lies ahead.
